title: Peak concentration and time to peak after one oral dose

segs.text: Module five, objective three. The peak concentration and the time to peak after a single oral dose. t max is the time after the dose at which the plasma concentration is highest, and C max is that highest concentration. Before the peak, absorption is faster than elimination, so the level rises. At the peak the rate in equals the rate out. After it, elimination is faster, so the level falls.

card.m: t<sub>max</sub>: time of the peak, hr   C<sub>max</sub>: the peak, mg/L
before t<sub>max</sub>: rate in > rate out
at t<sub>max</sub>: rate in = rate out
after t<sub>max</sub>: rate out > rate in

segs.text: The time of the peak depends only on the two rate constants, k a and k. The dose, F and V D multiply every point of the curve by the same number, so they raise or lower the whole curve together and cannot move the time of its peak. She said, t max depends solely on k and k a. A larger k a brings drug in faster, so the peak comes earlier and is higher; in a textbook problem, the formulation with the larger k a reaches its peak about an hour sooner. A larger k also brings the peak earlier, but lower, because drug leaves faster and the level cannot build as high.

card.m: D<sub>0</sub>, F, V<sub>D</sub>: scale the whole curve; t<sub>max</sub> unchanged
k<sub>a</sub> up → t<sub>max</sub> earlier, C<sub>max</sub> higher
e.g. (Ch 16) k 0.3 hr<sup>−1</sup>: k<sub>a</sub> 1 hr<sup>−1</sup> → ≈ 1.7 hr; k<sub>a</sub> 0.45 hr<sup>−1</sup> → ≈ 2.7 hr
k up → t<sub>max</sub> earlier, C<sub>max</sub> lower

segs.text: Because only the two constants matter, swapping them gives the same t max. In the textbook table, a k a of zero point one with a k of zero point two per hour, and a k a of zero point two with a k of zero point one, both peak at six point nine three hours. C max and A U C differ, though, because k, which sets the clearance, has changed.

card.m: swap k<sub>a</sub> and k → same t<sub>max</sub>
k<sub>a</sub> 0.1, k 0.2 and k<sub>a</sub> 0.2, k 0.1 hr<sup>−1</sup>: t<sub>max</sub> 6.93 hr both (Ch 16 Table 16-2)
C<sub>max</sub> 2.50 vs 5.00 mcg/mL; AUC 50 vs 100 mcg·hr/mL

segs.text: t max equals the natural log of k a over k, divided by k a minus k. Only rate constants appear, so a dose change cannot move t max, and swapping k a and k turns both the log and the difference negative, so the signs cancel and t max is the same. There is no separate C max line for a single oral dose: t max is put in for t in the C p equation, which is why t max always comes first. She said, If you are asked for C max, and I will ask you for C max, you must find t max first. Both lines need rate constants, not half-lives, in the same time unit.

card.m: swap: ln(k ÷ k<sub>a</sub>) = −ln(k<sub>a</sub> ÷ k),   k − k<sub>a</sub> = −(k<sub>a</sub> − k)
C<sub>max</sub> = {{frac:F k<sub>a</sub> D<sub>0</sub>|V<sub>D</sub> (k<sub>a</sub> − k)}} × (e<sup>−k t<sub>max</sub></sup> − e<sup>−k<sub>a</sub> t<sub>max</sub></sup>)

segs.text: Her slide Example one: V D is twenty two liters, the absorption half-life forty five minutes, the elimination half-life three hours, and F eighty five percent, and the peak after a single five hundred milligram dose, and its time, are asked. t max comes first, so both half-lives go to hours and then to rate constants: k a is zero point nine two four and k is zero point two three one per hour. k a is four times k, and t max comes out at two hours.

card.m: V<sub>D</sub> = 22 L, t½<sub>a</sub> = 45 min, t½ = 3 hr, F = 0.85, D<sub>0</sub> = 500 mg

segs.text: Then C max is the C p equation at two hours, and the fraction in front needs V D. She said, Do not forget the volume of distribution. The fraction is twenty five point seven six milligrams per liter, and the bracket at two hours is zero point four seven two four. C max is twelve point one seven milligrams per liter, two hours after the dose. The peak is below the fraction in front, as on every oral curve, because the bracket, drug in minus drug out, is less than one.

When the equation is given already worked out, the exponents give the constants and the same two answers follow. In her Example two, k a is two point seven five and k zero point two two per hour, so t max is one hour, and one hour in the given equation gives a C max of fifty five point four milligrams per liter. Her in class practice two, twenty three point two times the bracket of e to the minus zero point one eight two t and e to the minus zero point eight seven two t, gives a t max of two point two seven hours and a C max of twelve point one four milligrams per liter.

Quiz three asked what is true of the time to reach the maximum concentration, and the key is that it depends on the absorption and elimination rate constants, not on the dose. Another quiz item gave a dose, F and V D that were not needed; its half-lives of zero point eight and five point six hours give a t max of two point six hours. In her practice one, the one point five hours is the absorption half-life, so k a is zero point six nine three over one point five hours, zero point four six two per hour. Absorption half-lives often come in minutes and go to hours first, and leaving V D out of the fraction is the other common error.
